overallAssessment.verdict: data/regions/pembrokeshire.ts is a well-structured, richly detailed location data file with hero copy, key facts, seasonal guide, insider tips, 12 top experiences, 10 FAQs, hidden gems, and food listings. However it cites 'Perplexity research' as its primary source — AI-generated content — which violates the site's no-AI-content policy. All pricing figures (8 experience price ranges), the transport claim about New Quay dolphin trips, and several operational details (Skomer booking, bus routes) must be re-verified against official sources. Additionally the OG/social image referenced in the TS file (pembrokeshire-og.jpg) does NOT exist on disk, and the hero image has no provenance record in the image registry. One geographic error has been identified: 'Dolphin Watching from New Quay' mis-attributes a Ceredigion operator activity to Pembrokeshire.
overallAssessment.structuralQuality: HIGH — the TS data file is well-organised with all required sections. Strong editorial voice that captures Pembrokeshire's coastal identity. Suitable as the canonical source once claims are verified.
overallAssessment.factualConfidence: MEDIUM — national park designation, coast path length, key geography, heritage, and wildlife facts are stable and accurate. All pricing, transport details, and one geographic claim (New Quay dolphin trips) require human verification.

criticalIssues.issue: Geographic error — 'Dolphin Watching from New Quay' is a Ceredigion activity, not Pembrokeshire
criticalIssues.diagnosis: New Quay (Cei Newydd) is a village in Ceredigion county, not in the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park. It lies north of the Teifi estuary and north of the Pembrokeshire/Ceredigion border. Attributing New Quay dolphin boat trips to a Pembrokeshire location landing page is geographically incorrect and could mislead visitors who navigate to the wrong region. The Cardigan Bay bottlenose dolphins are real, but the primary Pembrokeshire shore-based dolphin watching site is Strumble Head (Fishguard area), not New Quay. Pembrokeshire Coast National Park's own wildlife information does not reference New Quay dolphin trips.

verified_or_stable.claim: Pembrokeshire Coast National Park — Britain's only coastal national park, established 1952
verified_or_stable.note: The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park was established on 29 February 1952, making it the third national park in Wales and England. It is the only national park in the UK designated primarily for its coastline.

verified_or_stable.claim: Welsh name: Sir Benfro
verified_or_stable.note: Sir Benfro is the correct Welsh-language name for the county of Pembrokeshire.
verified_or_stable.source: https://www.pembrokeshire.gov.uk/ (site uses Sir Benfro / Pembrokeshire bilingual branding)

verified_or_stable.claim: Pembrokeshire Coast Path: 186 miles
verified_or_stable.note: The official Pembrokeshire Coast National Park and Wales Coast Path websites confirm the Pembrokeshire Coast Path is 186 miles / 299 km. Well-established official measurement.

verified_or_stable.claim: National Park area: 240 sq miles / 620 km²
verified_or_stable.note: The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park covers 620 km² (240 sq miles). This figure is stated by PCNP and is geographically stable.

verified_or_stable.claim: Highest point: Foel Cwmcerwyn 536m in the Preseli Hills
verified_or_stable.note: Foel Cwmcerwyn (536m) is the highest point in the Preseli Hills and in Pembrokeshire. Geographically stable, well-documented.

verified_or_stable.claim: St Davids — Britain's smallest city, population ~1,600, medieval cathedral
verified_or_stable.note: St Davids was granted city status in 1994 (having held it historically) and is recognised as the smallest city in Britain by area and population. The cathedral is 12th-century, founded on the site of St David's monastery. Population ~1,600 is a commonly cited and stable figure for the city itself.

verified_or_stable.claim: Preseli Hills bluestones — source of Stonehenge's inner stones
verified_or_stable.note: Geological and archaeological research has confirmed that the bluestones of Stonehenge's inner circle originated from the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire, specifically the Carn Goedog and Rhosyfelin outcrops. Well-documented in peer-reviewed research.

verified_or_stable.claim: Skomer Island — puffins nesting April-July
verified_or_stable.note: Skomer Island is managed by the Wildlife Trust of South and West Wales. Puffins arrive in April and depart by late July. The island hosts one of the largest puffin colonies in southern Britain. Booking via Wildlife Trust is the correct mechanism.

verified_or_stable.claim: Cardigan Bay bottlenose dolphins — resident population, Special Area of Conservation
verified_or_stable.note: Cardigan Bay is designated a SAC (Special Area of Conservation) partly for its resident bottlenose dolphin population. Shore-based watching from Strumble Head is a well-established activity within Pembrokeshire.

verified_or_stable.claim: Strumble Head — best shore-based dolphin watching in Wales
verified_or_stable.note: Strumble Head is consistently cited by Wildlife Trust of South and West Wales and PCNP as one of the best places in Wales for shore-based dolphin watching. The lighthouse and headland are within the national park boundary. 'Dolphin o'clock' phrasing is local vernacular.

verified_or_stable.claim: Abereiddy Blue Lagoon — flooded slate quarry
verified_or_stable.note: Abereiddy's Blue Lagoon (also written 'Blue Lagoon' or 'The Blue Lagoon') is a former slate quarry flooded by the sea. Well-documented site within the national park. Free parking description is consistent with current visitor information.

verified_or_stable.claim: Freshwater West — consistent surf beach
verified_or_stable.note: Freshwater West is the most exposed west-facing beach in Pembrokeshire and consistently receives the best surf. No lifeguard service (important safety note). Description as 'premier surf beach' is consistent with all surf forecasting and visitor sources.

verified_or_stable.claim: Pembrokeshire Coast Path cumulative elevation claim '35,000ft (more than Everest)'
verified_or_stable.note: The 35,000ft (c.10,700m) cumulative ascent claim is a widely-cited statistic used by Visit Pembrokeshire and PCNP in promotional materials. The comparison to Everest (8,849m) is an approximation — the path undulates more than Everest in total ascent, not altitude. The figure is plausible and commonly stated, though the exact measurement varies slightly by source. Safe to publish as an approximation with standard care about the 'more than Everest' framing.

verified_or_stable.claim: Skomer, Skokholm, Ramsey, Caldey islands
verified_or_stable.note: All four are real islands off the Pembrokeshire coast. Skomer (Wildlife Trust), Skokholm (Wildlife Trust), Ramsey (RSPB), Caldey (Cistercian monastery). Well-documented.

verified_or_stable.claim: Caldey Island — monastery visit, monk-made chocolate and perfume
verified_or_stable.note: Caldey Island is home to a Cistercian monastery. The monks do produce perfume and chocolate, sold in the gift shop. Boat trips operate from Tenby. The monastery and visitor facilities are well-documented.

verified_or_stable.claim: Porthgain — former slate port
verified_or_stable.note: Porthgain is a former industrial harbour that exported slate and crushed stone. The Sloop Inn and The Shed (previously The Granary and then The Shed Fish Bistro) are real and well-established businesses at the harbour.

verified_or_stable.claim: Manorbier Castle — medieval, visible on coastal section
verified_or_stable.note: Manorbier Castle is a real 12th-century Norman castle managed by a private family. It overlooks the beach and is visible from the coast path. Described as 'best situated in Wales' by medieval writer Gerald of Wales.

verified_or_stable.claim: TYF Adventure and Preseli Venture — coasteering operators at St Davids
verified_or_stable.note: TYF Adventure (also TYF Group) is the operator credited with founding coasteering as a commercial activity in the 1980s at St Davids Head. Preseli Venture is another established outdoor activity centre near St Davids. Both are real operators with websites.

verified_or_stable.claim: Gwaun Valley — uses pre-1752 Julian Calendar for new year celebrations
verified_or_stable.note: The Gwaun Valley (Cwm Gwaun) near Fishguard is well-known for celebrating the new year on 13 January according to the old Julian calendar, a tradition maintained since the calendar change of 1752. Well-documented local tradition.

verified_or_stable.claim: Ceibwr Bay — Wales' tallest sea cliffs and Witches' Cauldron
verified_or_stable.note: Ceibwr Bay is a shingle beach near Moylgrove in north Pembrokeshire with dramatic folded rock strata cliffs. The nearby 'Witches' Cauldron' (Pwll y Wrach) is a collapsed sea cave/natural arch. Well-documented by PCNP and coast path guides.

verified_or_stable.claim: 13 Blue Flag beaches — more than any other Welsh county
verified_or_stable.note: Blue Flag status is awarded annually (results typically announced in May). The claim that Pembrokeshire has 13 Blue Flag beaches and more than any other Welsh county has been accurate in recent years. Verify the 2026 award list before publishing.

verified_or_stable.claim: 50+ beaches
verified_or_stable.note: PCNP and Visit Pembrokeshire consistently reference 50+ beaches in the national park area. The exact count varies by how 'beach' is defined (some coves are very small) but 50+ is a widely used and defensible approximation.

Pembrokeshire boat operators (Venture Jet for example) operate from St Davids/Solva area.

blockers.blocker: Geographic error — 'Dolphin Watching from New Quay' and Mwnt reference are Ceredigion activities, not Pembrokeshire
blockers.detail: topExperiences[5] lists 'Dolphin Watching from New Quay' with a price range and '95%+ success rate'. New Quay is in Ceredigion county, north of the Pembrokeshire/Ceredigion border, not within the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park. The FAQ (faqs[8]) also cites 'New Quay' and 'Mwnt' as Pembrokeshire dolphin-watching sites — both are geographically incorrect. This is a content accuracy error that will mislead visitors trying to plan a Pembrokeshire trip.
blockers.resolution: Remove the 'Dolphin Watching from New Quay' experience entirely. Replace with a Pembrokeshire-based wildlife activity (e.g. wildlife boat trips from Pembrokeshire operators, seal watching at Ramsey Island, or a Strumble Head shore-based dolphin watching entry). Update FAQ to reference only Strumble Head (and other Pembrokeshire-specific spots) and remove the New Quay and Mwnt references. Source for Strumble Head: https://www.pembrokeshirecoast.wales/wildlife/marine-wildlife/
